en.title: X-Men '97 Season 2 Episode 6 Embraces Evolution and Danger
en.summary: After a tumultuous first half of the season, the X-Men attempt a return to normalcy, only to be confronted by new threats and uncomfortable truths. The latest episode dives deep into mutant evolution and the ever-present menace that defines the team.
en.body:
The X-Men are back in session, but 'business as usual' is a concept that seems to elude mutantkind. Following the seismic events of the season's first half, **X-Men '97** Season 2 Episode 6, titled "Danger.exe," sees the team attempting to recalibrate. Storm steps into the role of headmistress at the Xavier's School for Gifted Children, welcoming a vibrant student body that includes comic favorites like Doop, Shark Girl, Eye Boy, Glob Herman, and the often-troublesome Quentin Quire. The roster also expands with the full-time addition of Bishop and Polaris, who finds a new home after her departure from X-Factor due to her dwindling patience with Reverend Stryker's Purifiers.

However, the illusion of normalcy is shattered as the episode delves into the inherent dangers of mutation and evolution. The narrative embraces concepts that push the boundaries of what it means to be an X-Man, drawing inspiration from pivotal comic eras. The episode invokes the spirit of **Grant Morrison's** influential 2001 reinvention of the X-Men, as well as the ambitious Krakoa era launched by **Jonathan Hickman** in 2019. These storylines fundamentally challenged the status quo and explored the complex future of mutantkind.

"Danger.exe" doesn't shy away from the darker, more unsettling aspects of the mutant experience. It integrates elements from **Joss Whedon's** run on *Astonishing X-Men*, particularly the menacing antagonist known as Danger. The episode forces the X-Men into a hellish, simulated environment designed to terrify and attack them. When the team outside believes they've neutralized the threat by destroying the room's CPU, they inadvertently release the sentient intelligence, allowing it to manifest a physical form and adopt the name Danger. This narrative turn underscores a core tenet of the X-Men: they represent the next stage of human evolution, and while they strive for harmony, they are also prepared to evolve their tactics when faced with relentless oppression.

## Embracing a Legacy of Evolution

The episode's visual language also pays homage to significant comic moments, with the X-Men sporting biker-style costumes reminiscent of **Frank Quitely's** designs for Morrison's run. This aesthetic choice is more than just a nod to the past; it signifies the team's ongoing adaptation and their willingness to embrace new identities and challenges. The integration of these iconic comic elements, coupled with the introduction of new characters and the exploration of mature themes, solidifies **X-Men '97** as a series that respects its rich history while boldly forging its own path.

## The Uncomfortable Truth of Mutant Identity

The X-Men have always been more than just superheroes; they are a metaphor for marginalized groups, constantly fighting for acceptance in a world that fears and hates them. "Danger.exe" amplifies this discomfort by showcasing how even the X-Men's sanctuary can become a source of peril. The episode forces the team to confront their own limitations and the ever-present threat that their own powers, or external forces, can turn against them. This mirrors the core X-Men philosophy: the best stories should make us uncomfortable, forcing us to question the nature of prejudice, evolution, and the price of peace.

## What's Next

With the sentient Danger now a physical entity and the X-Men facing internal and external threats, the stakes for the remainder of **X-Men '97** Season 2 are higher than ever. Fans can anticipate further exploration of the new mutant students and the evolving dynamics within the team as they grapple with this formidable new adversary. The episode, titled "Danger.exe," is scheduled to air on Disney+ on July 22, 2026.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for X-Men ’97 season 2 episode 6 . The X-Men should make us uncomfortable. Where the Avengers or Justice League exist only to protect us and inspire us, the X-Men represent the next stage of human evolution. Yes, they’re willing to protect a world that hates and fears them and, yes, they’ll pursue a dream of humans and mutants living in harmony. But people can only be pushed so far, and the X-Men are no different. The best X-Men stories should also have a sense of menace, the realization that they’ll shift tactics to protect themselves if humanity continues to oppress them. In its best moments, “Danger.exe” invokes that sense of danger, especially at the end, when it invokes both Grant Morrison ‘s reinvention from 2001 and the Krakoa era that Jonathan Hickman launched in 2019, two of the most daring approaches to Marvel ‘s mutants. But the episode invokes a different sort of discomfort by integrating concepts and scenes from Joss Whedon ‘s Astonishing X-Men run, including the villain Danger. “Danger.exe” sees the team trying to get back to business as usual after the events of the first half of the season. Class is back in session at Xavier’s School for Gifted Children, with Storm taking over as headmistress and a student body that includes some favorites from the comics (Doop! Shark Girl! Eye Boy! Glob Herman! ugh, Quentin Quire). We even have new members in the form of Bishop, finally here full time, and Polaris, who gets booted from X-Factor after her patience with Reverend Stryker’s Purifiers. Yet, the X-Men have no normal, and must always evolve. So, in addition to adopting the biker-style costumes that Frank Quitely designed for Morrison’s run, Xavier rethinks his dream. By the end of the episode, he has transitioned his focus away the school and launches X-Corp. The episode doesn’t entirely explain what X-Corp is, and knowledge of the comics doesn’t help much. But Val Cooper’s irritation at the end indicates that Xavier’s making a play for international sovereignty, not unlike Krakoa. In short, a lot happens in “Danger.exe,” as has been the case for every episode of X-Men ’97 . For as much as last week’s “ Weapon X, Lies, and DVDs ” too quickly glossed over important character details, “Danger.exe” hits just the right combination of spectacular action and character attention. The episode deftly blends character progression with plot beats, making room for the big set-pieces. We see that precision in the first scene, in which Xavier uses the Danger Room to relive the final moments of Magneto’s life.
